title: The Inversion of Greatness: From the Nature of Necessity to Maximum Possibility
description:
The Inversion of Greatness is an analytic work in modal metaphysics: a complete argument, derived step by step. Its headline thesis is the Necessity of Nature (structural naturalism).

The classical traditions asked what, if anything, exists necessarily, and answered with a maximally great being—a God outside time, space, and substance, the source of everything possible. This book argues they asked the right question and misplaced the answer.

Most arguments that reach a necessary being help themselves to S5 and move on. This one derives it first, from Reality’s having no beyond and real possibility’s being Reality’s single complete range rather than a local accessibility relation, with modal bivalence fixing the two verdicts as exhaustive. It then argues from the actuality of change—witnessed in reflection and independently in movement—that any genuine change requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and bearing across change. Those three conditions hold of necessity, and their joint structure is what the book calls Nature. Naturalism gets a derived structural ground rather than a brute starting point.

From there: no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits, blocking a divine intellect along with every other occupant of that domain. Essence-prior, analogical, and apophatic proposals secure no place outside Nature either: whatever does concrete work stands in the conditions, whatever retains determinate abstract content is structure of Nature, and whatever withdraws all determinate content fails specification. Any possible referent is Nature or an aspect of it, there is no supernature, and Reality is nothing over and above Nature. Every attempt to place a separate domain outside it faces the same price: affirming a difference that is a difference in nothing, or denying that what tells things apart is structure—and a God said to differ from that structure only by existing in itself differs only as pure act, which either has structure or is Nature under another name.

The inversion isn’t greatness changing owners. At the level of metaphysical ultimacy, necessity, eternity, and self-subsistence belong to Nature’s own structure, without making Nature a mind or a moral subject. Tested one at a time, personal attributes—knowing, being present, being moved by another, holding to a character through change—require the conditions wherever they carry determinate content, and dissolve into specification failure only when every content-bearing articulation is withdrawn. Rather than sanctifying Nature, the book relocates structural ultimacy to Nature and leaves evaluative and personal predicates with the subjects who exercise them.

The later parts carry the framework outward—to physics, where the cosmological singularity marks a boundary of description rather than a boundary of being (with the cosmic cycle conditional on stated physical premises); to consciousness, which belongs to Nature’s structure, since no complete structural duplicate of a feeling organism lacks the feeling, and is identified by best explanation as a living organization registering itself from within; and to a politics built on what claiming authority commits an institution to, widening effective access—maximum shared possibility—by degree on a foundation of material and civic conditions without enlarging Reality’s modal range. A closing part tests classical Abrahamic doctrines, including the problem of evil, internally against their own commitments alongside the attribute results of Chapters 10–11.
